nameStory: This rare wildflower is named after William Robbins, an early botanist who first collected specimens in Vermont in the 1800s. The "milkvetch" part comes from an old belief that livestock grazing on these plants would produce more milk, though this isn't actually true!
description: Robbins' Milkvetch is a small, low-growing perennial wildflower that hugs close to the ground in a cushion-like form. It rarely gets taller than 6 inches, with compound leaves made up of many small leaflets that give it a delicate, feathery appearance. In summer, it produces clusters of small purple or white pea-like flowers that are typical of the legume family. This is one of New England's rarest plants, found in only a handful of locations.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pea-like flowers in shades of purple, pink, or white, clustered together on short stems. Each flower has the classic legume shape with an upper 'banner' petal and lower 'keel' - they feel papery when gently touched.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 7-15 small, oval leaflets arranged along a central stem. The leaflets feel soft and slightly fuzzy, almost velvety to the touch, and are grayish-green in color.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, dense mats or cushions that spread horizontally rather than growing tall. The entire plant rarely exceeds 6 inches in height and has a sprawling, carpet-like appearance.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops small, inflated pods that rattle when shaken once the seeds are mature. The pods are hairy and feel slightly papery, containing several small, hard seeds inside.

habitat: In New England, Robbins' Milkvetch is extremely rare and found only in very specific rocky habitats along riverbanks, particularly limestone outcrops and gravelly shores of the Connecticut River. It prefers well-drained, alkaline soils in areas that flood occasionally but dry out completely. You'll only find it in a few protected locations in New Hampshire and Vermont.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small, fuzzy leaflets unfurl from the base. Plants begin forming their characteristic low mats as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from June through August, when the distinctive pea-like flowers appear. This is the best time for identification when flowers are most visible.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and turn brown, often persisting on the plant. Leaves may begin to yellow but the plant remains visible.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only dead stems and possibly some persistent seed pods. Nearly impossible to identify during dormant season.

funFact: Robbins' Milkvetch is so rare that one variety (var. jesupii) is federally endangered with only three known populations left in the entire world - all along a tiny stretch of the Connecticut River!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small legumes like wild lupines or vetches, but Robbins' Milkvetch's extremely low, mat-forming growth habit sets it apart - remember 'Robbins stays close to the riverbank rocks' since it never gets tall like other pea family plants.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'milkvetch,' these plants don't actually increase milk production in livestock - this is an old folk belief. The scientific name honors Samuel Robbins, but the common name sometimes gets confused with other botanists of the same era.
compareHints: Unlike Alpine Milkvetch which grows in high mountain areas, Robbins' Milkvetch is found at low elevations along rivers. Canadian Milkvetch grows much taller (up to 3 feet) while Robbins' stays under 6 inches. Chickpea Milkvetch has more rounded leaflets, whereas Robbins' has narrow, oval ones with a distinctly fuzzy texture.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Alpine Milkvetch differs from its cousin Canadian Milkvetch by being much shorter and growing only in alpine zones, while Canadian Milkvetch grows tall in lowland prairies and fields.
Canadian milkvetch is much more robust and tall than its rare New England relatives like Robbins' milkvetch, which is a tiny alpine plant, or Alpine milkvetch, which stays close to the ground.
Among New England's milkvetches, chickpea milkvetch is the most robust and bushy, staying under 3 feet tall.
